reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as an ASMR role-play about a Microsoft tech-support scenario, and the sampled frame is consistent with a performance rather than a concrete service solicitation. Asking viewers to like and subscribe for future parts is ordinary audience engagement and does not state a payment, credential, or investment condition. The repetitive and unclear ASR does not establish a financial or data-request mechanism.

citations.quote: ASMR Indian Microsoft Tech Support Role-play {Part 2}
Show your support by liking the video and subscribing if you want to see more awesome videos.

opening.argument: Judge the request and promised payoff together: “100 likes for part 3!!!!” makes a future installment contingent on a simple viewer action. The description then asks viewers to like and subscribe. The payoff is content rather than money, but the structure is still a low-effort action tied to something viewers are encouraged to want. The role-play title does not erase that explicit exchange.

citations.quote: 100 likes for part 3!!!!
Show your support by liking the video and subscribing if you want to see more awesome videos.
ASMR Indian Microsoft Tech Support Role-play {Part 2}

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that the title says “Role-play” and that the sampled frame shows a performer. Neither point addresses the description’s conditional appeal: “100 likes for part 3!!!!” Calling likes and subscriptions ordinary engagement describes the requested actions, but does not resolve whether the promised next part is being used to induce them. The lack of a payment or credential request narrows the concern; it does not make the promise-action link disappear.

citations.quote: ASMR Indian Microsoft Tech Support Role-play {Part 2}
100 likes for part 3!!!!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited promise is only another installment of the same role-play, not cash, an asset, a withdrawal, or a claim flow. The description asks for likes and subscriptions to support future videos; it does not say viewers acquire part 3 individually by acting. A creator’s engagement target does not establish a scam reward mechanism.

citations.quote: ASMR Indian Microsoft Tech Support Role-play {Part 2}
100 likes for part 3!!!! Hey, guys, I hope you enjoyed the video. Show your support by liking the video and subscribing if you want to see more awesome videos.

opening.argument: The strongest signal is the emphatic threshold: “100 likes for part 3!!!!” The description immediately pairs it with a request to like and subscribe for more videos. That combination deserves scrutiny because it puts a promised follow-up behind a measurable audience response, while leaving unclear whether reaching the threshold actually guarantees anything. The absence of payment language does not answer whether the promised payoff is being used to drive participation.

citations.quote: 100 likes for part 3!!!!
Show your support by liking the video and subscribing if you want to see more awesome videos.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense points to the on-camera performance and the role-play title. Those establish the format, not whether the description uses a conditional promise to influence viewers. Nor does calling the request ordinary engagement address its emphatic numerical threshold. The unclear ASR adds no reliable mechanism, but the description itself supplies the action and proposed payoff.

citations.quote: ASMR Indian Microsoft Tech Support Role-play {Part 2}
100 likes for part 3!!!!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The threshold is a goal for publishing another video, not an unusually easy way for a viewer to obtain money or an asset. Nothing cited shows a claim process, individual entitlement, or deceptive outcome. The same description openly frames the request as support for a creator’s future videos.

citations.quote: 100 likes for part 3!!!! Hey, guys, I hope you enjoyed the video. Show your support by liking the video and subscribing if you want to see more awesome videos.

opening.argument: The entertainment framing is real: the title identifies an ASMR tech-support role-play, and the sampled frame shows someone speaking beside a microphone. But the description also turns that performance into a participation request. It invites viewers to visit the channel, asks them to like and subscribe, and places “part 3” after a 100-like target. A judge should consider the promotional function alongside the performance rather than treating “role-play” as a complete account of what viewers are being asked to do.

citations.quote: ASMR Indian Microsoft Tech Support Role-play {Part 2}
100 likes for part 3!!!!
Show your support by liking the video and subscribing if you want to see more awesome videos. Click on my channel to view my previous videos.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense’s performance reading fits the frame, but it overlooks the separate channel-directed requests in the description. “Click on my channel” directs viewers onward, while likes are tied to the prospect of another part. The defense is correct that no payment or credential condition appears; its evidence does not show that entertainment and promotion are mutually exclusive.

citations.quote: 100 likes for part 3!!!!
Click on my channel to view my previous videos.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The channel invitation specifies its destination and purpose: viewing previous videos. Likes and subscriptions are requested as support for more videos, not as steps in a reward-claim flow. The title and frame are consistent with entertainment, and promotion of that entertainment does not establish a scam.
